summary: Defines Sieve extensions spamtest, spamtestplus and virustest, which give simple tests that match numeric scores for spam and viruses. The mail system does the actual checking. It replaces RFC 3685. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A spam checker gives each email a score. These extensions let mail rules read the score and decide what to do.

questions: filter spam by score in sieve
subtitle: Portable Sieve tests that read a spam or virus score instead of a scanner's own header format.

tldr.problem: Every spam or virus checker reports its result in its own header syntax, so each user's Sieve script ends up tied to one tool and stops being portable.
tldr.mechanism: The spamtest and virustest tests compare a normalized numeric score, supplied by the Sieve implementation, against values in the script, using the relational extension.
tldr.outcome: Scripts can filter on a generic score, such as 0 to 10 for spam or 0 to 5 for viruses. This RFC obsoletes RFC 3685 and adds a 0 to 100 percent scale.

today: RFC 5235 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3685, and the unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Generic Spam and Virus Tests
sections.content:
Sieve scripts are often used to filter spam and viruses. Usually a third-party checker handles the message first and adds a header whose syntax only that tool understands. Each user then writes a script that matches those headers, so the script has to stay in step with the tool and loses portability.

RFC 5235 introduces generic tests instead. The spam and virus checks themselves are done by the underlying Sieve implementation in whatever way suits it, and the script only sees a normalized result. Implementations MUST also support the Sieve relational extension (RFC 5231), because the tests rely on numeric comparison.
sections.plainLanguage: Every spam checker speaks its own language. These tests are a translator, so your filter rules work with any checker.

sections.title: The Normalized Result String
sections.content:
Both tests compare a normalized result string on the left-hand side with the value given in the script on the right. The string starts with a digit string whose numeric value falls in the range for that test. It may be followed by a space and arbitrary text, which can carry implementation-specific detail. Matching against that text with ordinary string comparators is possible, but it breaks portability.

Numbers are compared with the relational extension and the i;ascii-numeric comparator from RFC 4790, which looks only at the number at the start of the string. The :count match type tells a script whether any test was done at all: it returns 1 if the check ran and 0 if it did not, or if the implementation could not tell.

The RFC deliberately does not define what counts as spam or a virus, how to detect them, or what to do when one is found.
sections.plainLanguage: The checker writes a number on each email, maybe with a little note after it. Your rule only looks at the number.

sections.title: The spamtest Test
sections.content:
The usage is spamtest [":percent"] [COMPARATOR] [MATCH-TYPE] <value: string>. It is true when the normalized result matches the value, and the match type defaults to :is. The capability identifier is either spamtest or spamtestplus.

Without :percent, the score runs from 0 to 10. A 0 means the message was not tested, or Sieve could not tell. A 1 means it was tested and is clear of spam. Values 2 to 9 mean it may contain spam, with higher numbers meaning greater likelihood, and 10 means it definitely contains spam.

With :percent, the score runs from 0 to 100. Here 0 covers both clear of spam and not tested, 1 to 99 means it may be spam, and 100 means definitely spam. Using :percent requires the spamtestplus capability, and an implementation MUST return an error otherwise. Scripts SHOULD NOT name both spamtest and spamtestplus. To find out whether a message was tested when using percent, use :count or a plain :value test for 0.
sections.plainLanguage: The score is like a spiciness rating. A low number means mild, a high number means very spicy, and zero can mean nobody tasted it.

sections.title: Spamtest in a Script
sections.content:
The RFC's first example files untested mail and likely spam into separate mailboxes. A message with result 0 goes to INBOX.unclassified, and one with a value of 3 or more goes to INBOX.spam-trap.

The percent example uses spamtestplus and chains four outcomes. Untested mail goes to INBOX.unclassified, a percent score of 0 goes to INBOX.not-spam, anything below 37 goes to INBOX.spam-trap, and everything else is discarded. The RFC shows the same behavior written with :count for the first check.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like sorting mail into piles: not checked, safe, maybe junk, and straight to the bin.

sections.title: The virustest Test
sections.content:
The usage is virustest [COMPARATOR] [MATCH-TYPE] <value: string>, with the capability identifier virustest. It is true when the normalized result matches the value, defaulting to :is. The score runs from 0 to 5.

  • 0: not tested, or Sieve could not tell. This is also the result when no virus tool has categorized the message.
  • 1: tested and contains no known viruses.
  • 2: contained a known virus that was replaced with harmless content.
  • 3: contained a known virus that was cured so it is now harmless.
  • 4: possibly contains a known virus.
  • 5: definitely contains a known virus.

The example files untested mail into INBOX.unclassified, a result of 4 into INBOX.quarantine, and a result of 5 is discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: The virus score is a traffic light with extra steps: zero is not checked, one is clean, and five means definitely bad.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations SHOULD report spam and virus results only for messages that really went through a legitimate check. If the check depends on private header fields, the implementation must make sure a sender or intermediary cannot spoof them and trick the test into the wrong answer.

Administrators must keep virus checking tools up to date. Users should know that virustest is not a 100% reliable way to remove viruses and should stay careful with messages of unknown content and origin. Beyond this, the extensions raise no issues that are not already covered in RFC 5228.
sections.plainLanguage: A score is only trustworthy if nobody can fake the stamp. And even a good virus check can miss something, so be careful with strange emails.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 3685
sections.content:
RFC 5235 supersedes RFC 3685. The major changes are:

  • A :percent argument gives spamtest a new 0 to 100 range.
  • A spamtestplus requirement identifier indicates that extension in scripts.
  • The :count match type from RFC 5231 can now tell whether a message was tested.
  • It is clarified that "test not done" also covers the Sieve system being unable to tell whether a test was done.

For IANA, the registrations for spamtest and virustest replace those from RFC 3685, and spamtestplus is registered as a new capability name.
sections.plainLanguage: This version added a 0 to 100 scale, a new name to ask for it, and a clearer way to ask whether the email was checked at all.

items.label: Not tested
items.desc: Not tested, or Sieve could not tell.

items.label: Clean
items.desc: Tested and contains no known viruses.

items.label: Replaced
items.desc: Known virus replaced with harmless content.

items.label: Cured
items.desc: Known virus cured so it is now harmless.
